idiom_name: System.Threading.RateLimiting limiters (TokenBucket/SlidingWindow/FixedWindow) with ASP.NET Core AddRateLimiter/UseRateLimiter
implementation_notes: Microsoft ships the limiter itself: System.Threading.RateLimiting provides FixedWindowRateLimiter, SlidingWindowRateLimiter and TokenBucketRateLimiter - plus ConcurrencyLimiter, which bounds concurrent work rather than rate - and all of them hand out leases from AcquireAsync. ASP.NET Core supplies the enforcement surface: AddRateLimiter registers global or named policies, PartitionedRateLimiter.Create partitions by principal (user, API key, host), and UseRateLimiter or RequireRateLimiting applies them to endpoints, with the rejection response configured through RejectionStatusCode and OnRejected (the documentation's sample emits 429 plus Retry-After). QueueLimit = 0 makes the decision a refusal, which is the honest default when the caller can retry.
pitfalls: The default in-memory partition state is per process: behind several replicas the effective limit is multiplied unless a custom partitioned limiter backed by a shared store is supplied.
ConcurrencyLimiter is not a rate limiter - it caps in-flight requests, not requests per period; pairing them is common but they answer different questions.
The rejection status is not 429 by default: set RejectionStatusCode or an OnRejected callback deliberately, and emit Retry-After (the documented sample reads MetadataName.RetryAfter from the lease).
A global limiter still runs on endpoints that carry a named policy, so a per-endpoint policy does not replace the global limit.
